title: Decibels & Bode Plots
description: Express gains in dB, use logarithmic frequency scales and sketch straight-line Bode plots.

study.title: Decibels
study.body:
A transfer-function magnitude (a voltage ratio) is converted to decibels with 20 log; power ratios use 10 log. Magnitudes above 1 give positive dB, below 1 negative dB, and $|H| = 1$ is 0 dB. Going back: $|H| = 10^{|H|_{dB}/20}$.
Useful values: 10 → 20 dB, 2 → 6 dB, $\sqrt 2$ → 3 dB, $1/\sqrt 2$ → −3 dB, 0.1 → −20 dB, 0.01 → −40 dB.

study.title: Cascade connection
study.body: When the output of one two-port drives the input of the next, the overall transfer function is the product of the stage transfer functions, so in decibels the stage gains simply **add**. Pitfall: each $H_i$ must be found with the following stage attached, because loading changes it.

study.title: Logarithmic frequency scales
study.body: On a log axis equal distances mean equal frequency **ratios**. A **decade** is a factor 10 (e.g. 30 Hz to 300 Hz), an **octave** a factor 2 (e.g. 1 kHz to 2 kHz). The point halfway between $f_1$ and $f_2$ on a log axis is the geometric mean $\sqrt{f_1 f_2}$, not the arithmetic mean.

study.title: Bode magnitude plot
study.body: A Bode plot shows $|H|_{dB}$ versus log frequency. For the first-order lowpass $H = 1/(1 + jf/f_B)$ the curve follows two asymptotes: **0 dB** for $f \ll f_B$ and a line falling **−20 dB/decade** (−6 dB/octave) for $f \gg f_B$. They meet at the corner (break) frequency $f_B$, where the true curve is 3 dB below them.

study.title: Bode phase plot
study.body: Straight-line approximation of the lowpass phase $-\arctan(f/f_B)$: 0° below $f_B/10$, a line dropping 45° per decade from $f_B/10$ to $10f_B$ (−45° at $f_B$), and −90° above $10f_B$. The error is less than about 6°. A first-order **highpass** is the mirror image: magnitude rises +20 dB/decade below $f_B$ and is 0 dB above; phase goes from +90° to 0° (+45° at $f_B$).

study.title: Using the slope for design
study.body:
Because a first-order filter falls 20 dB per decade, an attenuation of $A$ dB needs the break frequency $A/20$ decades away from the unwanted component.
**Example:** to weaken a 50 kHz component by 40 dB with a lowpass, put $f_B$ two decades lower: 500 Hz. This also affects wanted signals nearby — sharper filters need higher order.

steps.title: Decibels
steps.body: Filter magnitudes can range from 100 down to 0.0001, so we express them in decibels. Magnitudes above 1 give positive dB, below 1 negative dB, and $|H| = 1$ is 0 dB. (Power ratios use 10 log instead of 20 log.)

steps.prompt: Express a transfer-function magnitude $|H| = {{H}}$ in decibels.
A filter's magnitude is {{D|dB}} at some frequency. What is $|H|$?
steps.explanation: Invert the definition: $|H| = 10^{|H|_{dB}/20}$ = 10^({{D}}/20) = 10^({{D/20}}) = {{10^(D/20)}}. Dividing by 10 instead of 20 is the power-ratio formula, which does not apply to voltage ratios.

steps.title: Cascades add in dB
steps.body: When stage 1 drives stage 2, the overall transfer function is the product $H = H_1H_2$. The log of a product is a sum of logs, so the dB values simply **add**. Caution: find $H_1$ with stage 2 connected, since loading changes it.

steps.prompt: Two stages are cascaded. Stage 1 has $|H_1| = {{a}}$ (with stage 2 connected) and stage 2 has $|H_2|_{dB}$ = {{G2|dB}}. Find $|H|_{dB}$ of the cascade.
steps.explanation: First convert stage 1: 20 log10({{a}}) = {{20*log10(a)|dB}}. In dB the stages add: {{20*log10(a)|dB}} + ({{G2|dB}}) = {{20*log10(a)+G2|dB}}.

steps.title: Logarithmic frequency scales
steps.body: On a log frequency axis, equal distances mean equal **ratios**. A **decade** is a factor of 10 in frequency; an **octave** is a factor of 2. Log scales let you see 10 Hz–20 Hz and 10 MHz–20 MHz on one plot.

steps.prompt: How many decades lie between {{f1|Hz}} and {{f2|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: Number of decades = log10($f_2/f_1$) = log10({{f2/f1}}) = {{log10(f2/f1)}}.

steps.prompt: Match each magnitude to its value in decibels.
steps.explanation: 20 log10(10) = 20, 20 log10(0.1) = −20, 20 log10(2) = 6.02, 20 log10(0.707) = −3.01 and 20 log10(1) = 0. Each factor of 10 is 20 dB, each factor of 2 about 6 dB.

steps.prompt: Which frequency is {{n}} octaves above {{f|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: Each octave doubles the frequency: {{f|Hz}} × 2^{{n}} = {{f|Hz}} × {{2^n}} = {{f*2^n|Hz}}. Multiplying by 10^{{n}} would be {{n}} decades; multiplying by 2 × {{n}} adds instead of compounding.

steps.title: Bode magnitude plot
steps.body: A Bode plot shows $|H|_{dB}$ on a log frequency axis. For the first-order lowpass $H = 1/(1 + jf/f_B)$ the curve follows two straight asymptotes: **0 dB** for $f \ll f_B$ and a line falling **−20 dB/decade** for $f \gg f_B$. They meet at the corner (break) frequency $f_B$.

steps.prompt: A first-order lowpass has $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}. Using the straight-line asymptote, estimate $|H|_{dB}$ at {{f|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: {{f|Hz}} is {{k}}·$f_B$, i.e. log10({{k}}) = {{log10(k)}} decades above $f_B$. At −20 dB/decade: −20 × {{log10(k)}} = {{-20*log10(k)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: Well above $f_B$, the magnitude of a first-order lowpass falls at a rate of …
steps.explanation: For $f \gg f_B$, $|H| \approx f_B/f$. A factor 10 in frequency divides $|H|$ by 10, which is −20 dB; a factor 2 divides it by 2, about −6 dB. So −20 dB/decade = −6 dB/octave. (−40 dB/decade belongs to second-order filters.)

steps.title: Corner error and phase
steps.body: The true curve is 3 dB below the asymptotes' corner at $f_B$ (and about 1 dB below at $f_B/2$ and $2f_B$). The phase $-\arctan(f/f_B)$ is approximated by: 0° below $f_B/10$, a line falling 45° per decade from $f_B/10$ to $10f_B$ (−45° at $f_B$), and −90° above $10f_B$.

steps.prompt: A first-order lowpass has $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}. Use the **straight-line** phase approximation to estimate $\angle H$ at {{f|Hz}}, in degrees.
steps.explanation: $f/f_B$ = {{m}}, so log10({{m}}) = {{log10(m)}} decades from $f_B$. The line passes −45° at $f_B$ with −45° per decade: $\angle H \approx$ −45° × (1 + {{log10(m)}}) = {{-45*(1+log10(m))}}°. (Exact: −arctan({{m}}) = {{-deg(atan(m))}}°.)

steps.prompt: The straight-line magnitude plot of a first-order lowpass is in error most at the break frequency, where the actual curve is 3 dB below the asymptotes.
steps.explanation: At $f = f_B$: $|H| = 1/\sqrt 2$, i.e. −3.01 dB, while both asymptotes give 0 dB. Moving away from $f_B$ the true curve approaches the asymptotes (≈ 1 dB error at $f_B/2$ and $2f_B$).

steps.prompt: Match each feature of a first-order **lowpass** Bode plot to its value.
steps.explanation: $H = 1/(1 + jf/f_B)$: at low $f$, $H \approx 1$ (0 dB, 0°); at $f_B$, $H = 1/(1+j)$ = 0.707∠−45° (−3 dB); at high $f$, $H \approx -jf_B/f$, falling 20 dB/decade with phase −90°.

steps.title: Highpass: the mirror image
steps.body: The first-order highpass $H = \frac{jf/f_B}{1 + jf/f_B}$ has the mirrored Bode plot: a low-frequency asymptote **rising +20 dB/decade** up to $f_B$, then 0 dB. Its phase goes from +90° (low $f$) through +45° at $f_B$ to 0°.

steps.prompt: A first-order highpass has $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}. According to its asymptotes, what is $|H|_{dB}$ at {{f|Hz}}?
steps.explanation: {{f|Hz}} is {{n}} decade(s) **below** $f_B$. Below $f_B$ the highpass asymptote rises at +20 dB/decade toward 0 dB at $f_B$, so going down {{n}} decade(s) gives {{-20*n|dB}}. (0 dB would be the passband; −3 dB applies only at $f_B$.)

steps.prompt: A transfer-function magnitude is {{D|dB}}. Find $|H|$ as a plain ratio.
A first-order lowpass has $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}. Find the **exact** $|H|_{dB}$ at {{f|Hz}}.
How many octaves lie between {{f1|Hz}} and {{f2|Hz}}?
Which frequency lies exactly halfway between {{f1|Hz}} and {{f2|Hz}} on a **logarithmic** frequency axis?
steps.explanation: Halfway on a log axis means equal ratios on both sides: $f_m/f_1 = f_2/f_m$, so $f_m = \sqrt{f_1 f_2}$ = √({{f1}} × {{f2}}) = {{sqrt(f1*f2)|Hz}}. (The linear midpoint {{(f1+f2)/2|Hz}} is not halfway on a log plot.)

steps.prompt: A first-order lowpass must reduce a {{f|Hz}} noise component by {{A}} dB. Using the −20 dB/decade asymptote, what break frequency $f_B$ is needed?
steps.explanation: {{A}} dB at 20 dB/decade is {{A/20}} decades, so $f_B$ must be a factor 10^{{A/20}} = {{10^(A/20)}} below the noise: $f_B$ = {{f|Hz}}/{{10^(A/20)}} = {{f/10^(A/20)|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: {{n}} identical first-order lowpass stages, each with $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}, are cascaded with buffers between them so they do not load each other. Find the overall $|H|_{dB}$ at {{f|Hz}}.
Measured on its own, stage 1 has −6 dB and stage 2 has −10 dB at some frequency. Connected directly (no buffer), the cascade measures −19 dB. What is the best explanation?
options: Stage 2 loads stage 1, so $H_1$ with stage 2 attached is not the stand-alone value
dB values of cascaded stages multiply instead of add
Decibels can only be added for power gains, not voltage gains
The measurement must be wrong; the cascade is always −16 dB
steps.explanation: $|H|_{dB} = |H_1|_{dB} + |H_2|_{dB}$ is always true, but $H_1$ must be evaluated **with stage 2 connected**. The input impedance of stage 2 loads stage 1 and here lowers its gain by an extra 3 dB. A buffer (e.g. a voltage follower) between the stages avoids this.

steps.prompt: A sinusoid with amplitude {{Vi|V}} at the input of an amplifier gives an output amplitude of {{Vo|V}}. What is the voltage gain in dB?
The graph is the Bode magnitude plot of a first-order lowpass filter. Read its break frequency $f_B$.
steps.hint: At $f_B$ the magnitude is 3 dB below its low-frequency level.
steps.explanation: The low-frequency (passband) level is {{K}} dB. At the break frequency the magnitude is 3 dB lower, {{K-3}} dB ($|H|$ down by a factor $1/\sqrt2$). The curve passes {{K-3}} dB at $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}. Check: one decade higher, at {{10*fB|Hz}}, it is about 20 dB below the passband ({{K-20}} dB).

steps.prompt: The graph shows the Bode magnitude plot of a lowpass filter. How steeply does it fall well above the corner frequency?
steps.explanation: Measure the drop over one decade well above the corner: from {{10*fB|Hz}} to {{100*fB|Hz}} the curve falls from about {{-20*n}} dB to {{-40*n}} dB, i.e. {{20*n}} dB per decade. Each first-order stage contributes −20 dB/decade, so this filter is of order {{n}}.

steps.prompt: The graph is the Bode magnitude plot of a filter. The input is a sinusoid with amplitude {{A|V}} at the marked frequency $f_{in}$ = {{f|Hz}}. Find the amplitude of the output.
steps.explanation: At $f_{in}$ the curve reads {{20*log10(H)}} dB. Convert to a ratio: $|H| = 10^{|H|_{dB}/20}$ = {{H}}. The output amplitude is $|H|\cdot V_{in}$ = {{H}} × {{A|V}} = {{A*H|V}}. (This is a highpass: below its corner it rises at +20 dB/decade, so a component {{-log10(m)}} decade(s) below the corner is attenuated by about {{-20*log10(m)}} dB.)

steps.prompt: The graph is the Bode **phase** plot of a first-order lowpass filter. Read its break frequency $f_B$.
steps.explanation: For a first-order lowpass $\angle H = -\arctan(f/f_B)$: 0° far below $f_B$, −90° far above, and exactly −45° at $f = f_B$. The curve crosses −45° at $f_B$ = {{fB|Hz}}.

steps.prompt: Which graph is the **phase** $\angle H$ of a first-order **highpass** filter? (Log frequency axis; the horizontal axis is 0°, the top and bottom edges are ±100°.)
steps.explanation: $H = \frac{jf/f_B}{1 + jf/f_B}$ has angle $90^\circ - \arctan(f/f_B)$: +90° far below $f_B$ (the output leads), +45° at $f_B$ and 0° far above. The curve from 0° down to −90° is the lowpass.
